newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Orbiting spacemen may drink to celebrate holiday.
newsitem.headline: Orbiting spacemen may drink to celebrate holiday.

text.p: The crew of the Mir orbiting space station, deprived of many of the pleasures of life on Earth, may have a drink to mark Russia's Space Day holiday on Saturday, an official said on Friday.
Also on Friday, Moscow's top space official said he had been promised government funding to continue Russia's commitment to the Alpha international space station, which will replace Mir.
Alcohol is officially banned on board Mir, but a space official who asked not to be named said cosmonauts sometimes have a few drops of cognac to celebrate an important occasion.

Even if they do sneak in a few sips, there will be no celebratory clinking of glasses. Because zero-gravity makes it impossible to drink from glasses, officials said the spacemen would take sips from a small flask.

Moderation is essential. Doctors at Russia's Medical and Biological Problems Research Institite, which supports the Mir programme, say just 50 to 100 grams of alcohol -- a big tumbler's worth -- would make one completely drunk in outer space.

A mission control spokesman said the two Russian cosmonauts and a U.S. astronaut would also have "more time to rest on Saturday and listen to their favourite music, which will be transmitted to Mir with congratulations from relatives and friends".
While the Mir crew relax in orbit, senior space officials on Earth are working overtime to pull the Russian space industry from deep crisis.
Thirty-six years after Yuri Gagarin's first manned space flight made the Soviet Union a leader in the space race, Russia's space programmes are in dire financial trouble.

Russian Space Agency Director Yuri Koptev met President Boris Yeltsin on Friday and said the government had promised to pay 1.5 trillion roubles ($261 million) in April and May to build a key segment of the Alpha station.
The Mir, which was launched 11 years ago, is scheduled to be replaced by the $37 billion Alpha project, but Russia has fallen behind on its contributions.
In February Moscow said it would have to postpone the first in a series of Alpha module launches, casting new doubts over Russia's continued ability to participate in the plan.
But Koptev said on Friday that if the government paid the promised $261 million, then Russia would meet its obligations.

Assessing Russia's space programme over the past five years, Yeltsin said that it "had fallen back from its achievements" because of inadequate funding. The president also ordered a direct communications link to be set up between the Kremlin and the space agency.
The new Alpha space station, to be completed by 2003, is being funded by the United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan.
Russia is also building the first module to go into orbit -- a cargo section -- and the third, the main living quarters.
Continued operation of Mir, however, is proving profitable for Russia. Last year Russia earned $471 million for hosting Western astronauts on Mir, Koptev said.

Russia has ambitious plans for the future. Itar-Tass news agency said that Moscow planned to send a probe to the moon in 1999 to test equipment to be used during a new mission to Mars expected in 2001.
